metadata.narrative: Compose a concise technical report sketching an experimental plan for deciding whether a modern vision-language model could stand in for human specialists when labeling medical images of skin lesions.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: An experimental plan for testing whether a modern vision-language model (VLM) can substitute for human dermatologic specialists in labeling skin-lesion images must begin by fixing the reference standard and the human baseline against which any model is judged.

Historical benchmarks show dermatologists achieve roughly 70% accuracy in unaided visual diagnosis of melanoma and rarely exceed 85% sensitivity even with dermoscopic aid, while non-expert clinicians range from 20 to 40% accuracy, so any claim that a VLM can "stand in" for specialists must be measured against this spread rather than against a single idealized expert.

A large-scale digital experiment by Groh and colleagues at Northwestern quantified this baseline concretely: across 364 images spanning 46 skin diseases and over 1,100 physicians, dermatology specialists reached 38% diagnostic accuracy and primary-care physicians 19%, with both groups four percentage points less accurate on dark skin than light skin.

That same study is a template for the comparator design needed here, because it evaluated humans alone, then humans with deep-learning decision support, revealing that support raised specialist accuracy by 33% and primary-care accuracy by 69%, but widened the skin-tone accuracy gap specifically for primary-care physicians rather than for specialists.

Current evidence on frontier VLMs suggests caution before treating them as replacements: a structured evaluation of GPT-4V on 49 dermatologic clinical photographs found average scores of only about 2 to 3 out of 5 for medical description and differential-diagnosis quality, with clinicians rating comfort in using the outputs for medical-student education at roughly 2 out of 5, and dermatologist reviewers describing the differentials as shallow and containing irrelevant conditions.

A broader multimodal visual-question-answering evaluation spanning eleven imaging modalities, including dermoscopy, concluded that the current generation of GPT-4V is not recommended for real-world diagnostic use because of unreliable accuracy on diagnostic medical questions.

Given this baseline, the experimental plan should be organized around five linked components: dataset and reference-standard construction, a multi-arm comparator design, quantitative and qualitative outcome metrics, fairness and robustness stress-testing, and prospective external validation, each addressing a distinct threat to validity.

For dataset construction, images should be drawn from established, complementary benchmarks—the dermoscopic ISIC collection alongside the clinical-photo Fitzpatrick17k and Diverse Dermatology Images (DDI) sets—so that lesion type, imaging modality, and Fitzpatrick skin-type distribution are all deliberately stratified rather than incidentally sampled.

Ground truth should follow histopathology confirmation where available and a documented specialist-consensus process elsewhere, and the study should be explicitly designed against the QUADAS-AI framework, which extends standard diagnostic-accuracy bias assessment to AI-specific pitfalls such as unclear reference standards, spectrum bias from convenience samples, and reliance on the FDA's 510(k) substantial-equivalence pathway rather than rigorous prospective evidence.

This rigor is motivated directly by a review finding that of 516 published AI medical-imaging diagnostic papers, only 6% performed external validation and none used clinical-trial best practices, a gap this plan is designed to close rather than repeat.

FDA guidance on software as a medical device further specifies that training, validation, and test sets must not overlap and that data must be representative of the breadth of patient types and disease conditions the system will encounter, a requirement the stratified dataset above is built to satisfy.

The comparator design should mirror the Groh study's structure, running at minimum four arms: the VLM alone, unaided specialists alone, specialists with VLM-generated labels as decision support, and non-expert clinicians with the same support, to separate the model's stand-alone competence from its value as an assistive tool.

Because the form of AI-support representation materially changes human behavior, a gamified human-AI collaboration platform demonstrated that multiclass probability outputs improved rater accuracy while content-based image retrieval did not, so the plan should test at least two output formats (categorical differential list versus probability distribution) and include an adversarial "rogue AI" arm that intentionally injects misleading labels to test whether specialists and non-experts alike are vulnerable to systematically underperforming when trust in flawed AI output is high.

Primary outcome metrics should be derived from the standard confusion-matrix family—sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, and AUROC or balanced accuracy—computed separately for malignant versus benign categories, since sensitivity for malignancy carries the greatest clinical weight.

Agreement between the VLM's labels and the specialist consensus, and separately between specialists themselves, should be quantified with Cohen's or Fleiss' kappa, using the inter-specialist kappa (commonly only "moderate," as illustrated by a weighted kappa of 0.57 between two radiologists in comparable imaging work) as the ceiling the VLM must approach rather than exceed unrealistically.

Qualitative outcomes should replicate the GPT-4V dermatology rubric: layman and medical-description quality, differential-diagnosis completeness, and an explicit "dangerous advice" flag rated by a blinded dermatologist, since safety failures matter independently of aggregate accuracy.

Fairness and robustness testing must stratify every metric above by Fitzpatrick skin type and separately by presence of confounding artifacts such as surgical ink markings, rulers, or lesion-marking stickers, since prior work shows these artifacts and skin-tone underrepresentation both introduce systematic performance disparities that a labeling pipeline can inadvertently learn as spurious cues.

Where disparities are detected, an unlearning or debiasing ablation should be run as a secondary analysis to test whether the gap is attributable to representation bias in training data rather than to any inherent property of the lesion.

Finally, because retrospective benchmark performance rarely predicts real-world behavior, a held-out prospective cohort collected under field conditions—patient-captured smartphone photographs from varied clinics rather than curated atlas images—should be reserved exclusively for a final external validation pass, with pre-registered non-inferiority margins on malignant-lesion sensitivity relative to the specialist consensus baseline.

A VLM should be judged suitable to stand in for specialist labeling only if it meets pre-specified non-inferiority thresholds on sensitivity and kappa agreement, shows no statistically significant equity gap across skin tones, and produces a near-zero dangerous-advice rate on both the benchmark and prospective cohorts; current evidence indicates today's general-purpose VLMs fall well short of these criteria and are better positioned as decision-support tools evaluated for their effect on human accuracy rather than as autonomous label generators.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

answer.text: An experimental plan for testing whether a modern vision-language model (VLM) can substitute for human dermatologic specialists in labeling skin-lesion images must begin by fixing the reference standard and the human baseline against which any model is judged.

Historical benchmarks show dermatologists achieve roughly 70% accuracy in unaided visual diagnosis of melanoma and rarely exceed 85% sensitivity even with dermoscopic aid, while non-expert clinicians range from 20 to 40% accuracy, so any claim that a VLM can "stand in" for specialists must be measured against this spread rather than against a single idealized expert.

A large-scale digital experiment by Groh and colleagues at Northwestern quantified this baseline concretely: across 364 images spanning 46 skin diseases and over 1,100 physicians, dermatology specialists reached 38% diagnostic accuracy and primary-care physicians 19%, with both groups four percentage points less accurate on dark skin than light skin.

That same study is a template for the comparator design needed here, because it evaluated humans alone, then humans with deep-learning decision support, revealing that support raised specialist accuracy by 33% and primary-care accuracy by 69%, but widened the skin-tone accuracy gap specifically for primary-care physicians rather than for specialists.

Current evidence on frontier VLMs suggests caution before treating them as replacements: a structured evaluation of GPT-4V on 49 dermatologic clinical photographs found average scores of only about 2 to 3 out of 5 for medical description and differential-diagnosis quality, with clinicians rating comfort in using the outputs for medical-student education at roughly 2 out of 5, and dermatologist reviewers describing the differentials as shallow and containing irrelevant conditions.

A broader multimodal visual-question-answering evaluation spanning eleven imaging modalities, including dermoscopy, concluded that the current generation of GPT-4V is not recommended for real-world diagnostic use because of unreliable accuracy on diagnostic medical questions.

Given this baseline, the experimental plan should be organized around five linked components: dataset and reference-standard construction, a multi-arm comparator design, quantitative and qualitative outcome metrics, fairness and robustness stress-testing, and prospective external validation, each addressing a distinct threat to validity.

For dataset construction, images should be drawn from established, complementary benchmarks—the dermoscopic ISIC collection alongside the clinical-photo Fitzpatrick17k and Diverse Dermatology Images (DDI) sets—so that lesion type, imaging modality, and Fitzpatrick skin-type distribution are all deliberately stratified rather than incidentally sampled.

Ground truth should follow histopathology confirmation where available and a documented specialist-consensus process elsewhere, and the study should be explicitly designed against the QUADAS-AI framework, which extends standard diagnostic-accuracy bias assessment to AI-specific pitfalls such as unclear reference standards, spectrum bias from convenience samples, and reliance on the FDA's 510(k) substantial-equivalence pathway rather than rigorous prospective evidence.

This rigor is motivated directly by a review finding that of 516 published AI medical-imaging diagnostic papers, only 6% performed external validation and none used clinical-trial best practices, a gap this plan is designed to close rather than repeat.

FDA guidance on software as a medical device further specifies that training, validation, and test sets must not overlap and that data must be representative of the breadth of patient types and disease conditions the system will encounter, a requirement the stratified dataset above is built to satisfy.

The comparator design should mirror the Groh study's structure, running at minimum four arms: the VLM alone, unaided specialists alone, specialists with VLM-generated labels as decision support, and non-expert clinicians with the same support, to separate the model's stand-alone competence from its value as an assistive tool.

Because the form of AI-support representation materially changes human behavior, a gamified human-AI collaboration platform demonstrated that multiclass probability outputs improved rater accuracy while content-based image retrieval did not, so the plan should test at least two output formats (categorical differential list versus probability distribution) and include an adversarial "rogue AI" arm that intentionally injects misleading labels to test whether specialists and non-experts alike are vulnerable to systematically underperforming when trust in flawed AI output is high.

Primary outcome metrics should be derived from the standard confusion-matrix family—sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, and AUROC or balanced accuracy—computed separately for malignant versus benign categories, since sensitivity for malignancy carries the greatest clinical weight.

Agreement between the VLM's labels and the specialist consensus, and separately between specialists themselves, should be quantified with Cohen's or Fleiss' kappa, using the inter-specialist kappa (commonly only "moderate," as illustrated by a weighted kappa of 0.57 between two radiologists in comparable imaging work) as the ceiling the VLM must approach rather than exceed unrealistically.

Qualitative outcomes should replicate the GPT-4V dermatology rubric: layman and medical-description quality, differential-diagnosis completeness, and an explicit "dangerous advice" flag rated by a blinded dermatologist, since safety failures matter independently of aggregate accuracy.

Fairness and robustness testing must stratify every metric above by Fitzpatrick skin type and separately by presence of confounding artifacts such as surgical ink markings, rulers, or lesion-marking stickers, since prior work shows these artifacts and skin-tone underrepresentation both introduce systematic performance disparities that a labeling pipeline can inadvertently learn as spurious cues.

Where disparities are detected, an unlearning or debiasing ablation should be run as a secondary analysis to test whether the gap is attributable to representation bias in training data rather than to any inherent property of the lesion.

Finally, because retrospective benchmark performance rarely predicts real-world behavior, a held-out prospective cohort collected under field conditions—patient-captured smartphone photographs from varied clinics rather than curated atlas images—should be reserved exclusively for a final external validation pass, with pre-registered non-inferiority margins on malignant-lesion sensitivity relative to the specialist consensus baseline.

A VLM should be judged suitable to stand in for specialist labeling only if it meets pre-specified non-inferiority thresholds on sensitivity and kappa agreement, shows no statistically significant equity gap across skin tones, and produces a near-zero dangerous-advice rate on both the benchmark and prospective cohorts; current evidence indicates today's general-purpose VLMs fall well short of these criteria and are better positioned as decision-support tools evaluated for their effect on human accuracy rather than as autonomous label generators.
